newsitem.title: USA: US High Court won't clarify insider lawsuit limits.
newsitem.headline: US High Court won't clarify insider lawsuit limits.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court refused Friday to clarify when the two-year statute of limitations begins in lawsuits to recover short-swing profits by a company insider.

At issue is whether the statute of limitations begins when the insider -- a director, officer or owner of more than 10 percent of a company's stock -- files the required report that discloses the short-swing transactions.
Short-swing transactions typically occur within a period of less than six months.

The federal securities law seeks to curb short-swing trading by insiders with confidential information, and allows a shareholder or corporation to sue over any such improper transactions to recover the profits.
The Supreme Court let stand a decision by a U.S. appeals court in New York that took a slightly different approach on when the statute of limitations begins.
The appeals court said the two-year limit can begin before the filing of the mandatory reports.
The case involved an appeal by Tristar Corp. It initially won nearly $183,000 against two officers and directors who engaged in short-swing transactions in 1989.
The appeals court overturned the award on the grounds that the lawsuit had been barred by the statute of limitations.
The high court's action was a setback for the U.S. Justice Department, which on behalf of the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the high court to hear the case.
